title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-313-385-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-313-385-001
Issues
Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
⮚
sustained injuries, including a L4 endplate fracture arising out of and in the
course of his employment on July 22, 2025.
If Claimant established that he suffered compensable injuries, whether he also
⮚
established, by a preponderance of the evidence, his entitlement to all
reasonable, necessary, and related medical treatment stemming from his July
22, 2025, work injury.
If Claimant established that he suffered compensable work-related injuries on
⮚
July 22, 2025, whether he also established, by a preponderance of the evidence,
that he is entitled to Temporary Total Disability (“TTD”) benefits beginning July
22, 2025, and ongoing.
If Claimant established that he suffered compensable injuries, what was his
⮚
Average Weekly Wage (AWW) on July 22, 2025.
Based on the evidence presented at hearing, the ALJ orders as follows:
Compensability
A. A “compensable injury” is one that requires medical treatment or causes
disability. Romero v. Industrial Commission, 632 P.2d 1052 (Colo. App. 1981);
Aragon v. CHIMR, et al., W.C. No. 4-543-782 (ICAO, Sept. 24, 2004); H & H
Warehouse v. Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167, 1169 (Colo. App. 1990). No benefits flow to
the victim of an industrial accident unless the accident results in a compensable
1

“injury.” Romero, supra; § 8-41-301, C.R.S. To sustain his burden of proof
concerning compensability, Claimant must establish that the condition for which
he seeks benefits was proximately caused by an “injury” arising out of and in the
course of employment. Loofbourrow v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 321 P.3d
548 (Colo. App. 2011), aff’d Harman-Bergstedt, Inc. v. Loofbourrow, 320 P.3d
327 (Colo. 2014); Section 8-41-301(I)(b), C.R.S.
B. The phrases "arising out of” and "in the course of" are not synonymous
and a claimant must meet both requirements for the injury to be compensable.
Younger v. City and County of Denver, 810 P.2d 647, 649 (Colo. 1991); In re
Question Submitted by U.S. Court of Appeals, 759 P.2d 17, 20 (Colo. 1988). The
latter requirement refers to the time, place, and circumstances under which a
work-related injury occurs. Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 381 (Colo. 1991).
C. An injury occurs in the course and scope of employment when it takes
place within the time and place limits of the employment relationship and during
an activity connected with the employee's job-related functions. In re Question
Submitted by U.S. Court of Appeals, supra; Deterts v. Times Publ'g Co., 38 Colo.
App. 48, 51, 552 P.2d 1033, 1036 (1976). Conversely, the "arising out of" test is
one of causation. It requires that the injury have its origins in an employee's
work-related functions and be sufficiently related thereto so as to be considered
part of the employee's service to the employer. Horodyskyj v. Karanian, 32 P.3d
470, 475 (Colo. 2001). Here, there is little question that Claimant’s alleged injury
occurred within the time and place limits of his employment, i.e. during a routine
workday and during an activity related to Claimant’s job duties as a skilled
construction laborer, namely adding an electrical circuit and switch to an existing
residential electrical service panel. Nonetheless, the question of whether
Claimant’s medical condition/symptoms and need for treatment arose out of his
employment must be answered before the injuries can be determined to be
compensable.
2

D. The determination of whether there is a sufficient "nexus" or causal
relationship between the Claimant's employment-related duties and the alleged
injury is one of fact, which the ALJ must determine based on the totality of the
circumstances. In Re Question Submitted by the United States Court of Appeals,
759 P.2d 17 (Colo. 1988); Moorhead Machinery & Boiler Co. v. Del Valle, 934
P.2d 861 (Colo. App. 1996). In this case, the totality of the evidence, including
Claimant’s testimony, supports the conclusion that he presented to the
Emergency Department (ED) at Parkview Pueblo West Hospital on July 22,
2025, after being electrocuted by three 110V wires as he was performing
electrical work at the direction of his boss, Shawn Moyers, who owns and
operates Timberline Custom Builders. Claimant was locked on to electrical
current and shocked for greater than 1 minute, suffered a loss of consciousness
and fell to the floor fracturing the endplate of his L4 vertebral body. (CHE 2).
Treatment for this injury included a kyphoplasty surgery performed by Dr. Craig
Lance on August 22, 2025. (CHE 6, p. 68). Claimant also developed
neuropathic pain, arrythmia and shortness of breath following his electrical
shock, which conditions required additional workup. (CHE 3-5). Based upon the
evidence presented, the ALJ is convinced that not only did Claimant’s injuries
occur within the time and place limits of his employment but also have their
origins in his work-related functions as a skilled laborer for Employer and are
sufficiently related to those functions (making electrical upgrades) so as to be
considered part of his service to Employer. Accordingly, the ALJ is persuaded
that Claimant’s injuries and need for treatment “arose out of” his work duties for
Employer. Because the ALJ is convinced that Claimant has established the
requisite nexus between his work activities and his July 22, 2025, injuries, the
claimed injuries are compensable.
Claimant’s Entitlement to Medical Benefits, Authorization and Right of Selection
3

E. Once a claimant has established the compensable nature of his/her work
injury, he/she is entitled to a general award of medical benefits and respondents
are liable to provide all reasonable, necessary, and related medical care to cure
and relieve the effects of the work injury. Section 8-42-101, C.R.S.; Grover v.
Industrial Commission, 759 P.2d 705 (Colo. 1988); Sims v. Industrial Claim
Appeals Office, 797 P.2d 777 (Colo. App. 1990). However, a claimant is only
entitled to such benefits as long as the industrial injury is the proximate cause of
his need for medical treatment. Merriman v. Indus. Comm’n, 210 P.2d 448 (Colo.
1949); Standard Metals Corp. v. Ball, 172 Colo. 510, 474 P.2d 622 (1970); § 8-
41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. Ongoing benefits may be denied if the current and ongoing
need for medical treatment or disability is not proximately caused by an injury
arising out of and in the course of the employment. Snyder v. City of Aurora, 942
P.2d 1337 (Colo. App. 1997). In other words, the mere occurrence of a
compensable injury does not require an ALJ to find that all subsequent medical
treatment and physical disability was caused by the industrial injury. To the
contrary, the range of compensable consequences of an industrial injury is
limited to those which flow proximately and naturally from the injury. Standard
Metals Corp. v. Ball, supra. As noted above, Claimant has proven that he
suffered compensable injuries to his low back and was treated for other injuries
associated with his electrocution through the ED at Parkview Pueblo West
Hospital and Drs. Sheldon Ravin, Stephen Farkas, and Craig Lance and their
referrals. The content of the medical records from the above-mentioned
providers combined with the testimony received at hearing persuades the ALJ
that the treatment Claimant received after his electrocution has been reasonable,
necessary and otherwise related to that mechanism of injury. Nonetheless, the
question of whether this treatment and the aforementioned providers was/were
authorized to treat Claimant must be addressed.
F. Authorization to provide medical care as part of a work-related claim refers
to a medical provider’s legal authority to provide treatment to the claimant with
4

the expectation that the provider will be compensated by the insurer for said
services. Bunch v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 148 P.3d 381 (Colo. App.
2006); One Hour Cleaners v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 914 P.2d 501
(Colo. App. 1995); In re Bell, W.C. No. 5-044-948-01 (ICAO, Oct. 16, 2018).
Medical services provided during a bona fide emergency are an exception to the
normal requirement that a claimant obtain authorization for all treatment
connected to the industrial injury. Larson's Workers' Compensation Law, §
94.02[6] (1999); Sims v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 797 P.2d 777 (Colo.
App. 1990). Otherwise, authorized providers include those medical personnel to
whom the claimant is directly referred by the employer, as well as providers to
whom an authorized provider refers the claimant in the normal progression of
care. Town of Ignacio v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 70 P.3d 513 (Colo.
App. 2002); City of Durango v. Dunagan, 939 P.2d 496 (Colo. App. 1997).
G. There is no precise legal test for determining what constitutes a medical
emergency.1 Rather, the question of whether a claimant established the
existence of a bona fide emergency is dependent on the particular facts and
circumstances of the claim. Timko v. Cub Foods, W. C. No. 3969-031 (June 29,
2005). In this case, the ALJ is persuaded that the intensity and duration of the
electrical shock Claimant sustained resulted in an emergent need to seek
medical treatment. Indeed, Claimant was shocked by multiple wires energized
with 110 volts of current, was unable to break the electrical connection and was
shocked for greater than one minute before the electrical current was cut. As
noted, before the current was cut, Claimant lost consciousness and fell to the
floor injuring his back. He was tachycardic, hypertensive and complaining of
chest pain and shortness of breath upon examination in the ED, raising concern
for cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial injury, rhabdomyolysis, internal burns/tissue
1 The exception is not limited to situations where life is threatened. Bunch v. Industrial Claim
Appeals Office of State of Colorado, 148 P.3d 381 (Colo.App.2006).
5

damage and neurologic injury as potential critical diagnoses. (CHE 2, p. 7). For
these reasons, the ALJ is convinced that Claimant suffered a bona fide medical
emergency and that the initial treatment rendered in the ED was reasonable and
necessary to evaluate the extent of damage caused by Claimant’s prolonged
electrical shock. Consequently, Claimant was not required to obtain prior
authorization from Respondent-Employer for this treatment.
H. Concerning the remainder of Claimant’s treatment, § 8-43-404(5) (a) (I)
(A), C.R.S. 2025, gives the employer has the right in the first instance to
designate the authorized provider to treat the claimant's compensable condition.
The rationale for this principle is that the employer and the employer’s insurance
carrier (respondents) may ultimately be liable for the claimant's medical bills and,
therefore, have an interest in knowing what treatment is being provided. Andrade
v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 121 P.3d 328 (Colo. App. 2005). The statute
requires the employer or insurer to "provide a list of at least four physicians . . .
in the first instance, from which list an injured employee may select the
physician who attends said injured employee." Similarly, Workers' Compensation
Rules of Procedure, Rule 8-2(A), 7 Code Colo. Reg. 1101-3, states that "[w]hen
an employer has notice of an on-the-job injury, the employer or insurer shall
provide the injured worker with a written list” of providers. In order to maintain
the right to designate a provider in the first instance, the employer has an
obligation to name the treating physician forthwith upon receiving notice of the
compensable injury. See Rogers v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 746 P.2d
545 (Colo. App. 1987). The failure to tender the "services of a physician . . . at
the time of injury" gives the employee "the right to select a physician or
chiropractor."
I. An employer's duty to designate is triggered once the employer or
insurer has some knowledge of facts that would lead a reasonably
conscientious manager to believe the case may involve a claim for
6

compensation. Bunch v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 148 P.3d 381 (Colo.
App. 2006); Jones v. Adolph Coors Co., 689 P.2d 681 (Colo. App. 1984);
Gutierrez v. Premium Pet Foods, LLC, W.C. No. 4-834-947 (ICAO, September 6,
2011). In this case, the evidence presented persuades the ALJ that Mr. Moyers
was present on the job site when Claimant was shocked, that he cut the power to
prevent further injury/death to Claimant and that he helped revive Claimant
before he was taken to the hospital for treatment. Accordingly, the ALJ is
convinced that Mr. Moyers was aware of Claimant’s accident and the work-
related nature of his injuries. The ALJ is also convinced that Mr. Moyers took no
action to designate a provider to attend to Claimant’s injuries following his initial
treatment in the ED at Parkview Pueblo West Hospital. Accordingly, the ALJ
concludes that the right to select a provider to treat Claimant’s injuries passed to
him. Based on the evidence presented, the ALJ finds that Claimant exercised
that right by initiating treatment with the providers at UCHealth Aspen Creek
Medical Center. As noted, authorized providers include those medical personnel
to whom the claimant is directly referred by an authorized provider in the normal
progression of care. Town of Ignacio v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, supra.
Thus, Dr. Craig Lance and those providers who performed diagnostic testing to
help delineate Claimant’s diagnosis are also authorized to treat Claimant. Based
on the evidence presented, the ALJ concludes that Respondent-Employer (Mr.
Moyers) is liable for the costs of any treatment rendered to Claimant by the
aforementioned providers, including the costs for any diagnostic testing based
upon the referrals of Drs. Russo, Rodgers, Ravin, Farkas, and Lance. Payment
shall be made in accordance with the Colorado Workers’ Compensation Medical
Benefits Fee Schedule. The Colorado Division of Workers’ Compensation can
help Employer calculate medical payments owed under the fee schedule.
Claimant’s Entitlement to Temporary Disability Benefits
7

J. To receive temporary disability benefits, Claimant must prove that his
injuries caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, that he left work
as a result of the disability, and that the disability resulted in an actual wage loss.
PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542 (Colo. 1995); City of Colorado
Springs v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 954 P.2d 637 (Colo. App. 1997).
Section 8-42-103(1), C.R.S. 2001; PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542
(Colo. 1995). As stated in PDM, the term "disability" refers to the claimant's
physical inability to perform regular employment. See also McKinley v. Bronco
Billy's, 903 P.2d 1239 (Colo. App. 1995). Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S., requires
Claimant to establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a
subsequent wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. PDM Molding, Inc. v.
Stanberg, supra. The term disability connotes two elements: (1) Medical
incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily function; and (2) Impairment
of wage-earning capacity as demonstrated by Claimant's inability to resume his
prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of
the earning capacity element of disability may be evidenced by a complete
inability to work, or by restrictions which impair the claimant's ability to effectively
and properly perform his/her regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy &
Co., 964 P.2d 595 (Colo. App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a
claimant must produce evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony
alone is sufficient to demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952
P.2d 831, 833 (Colo. App. 1997).
K. In this case, Claimant testified that he has not been returned to work by
his treating providers since being shocked on July 22, 2025. The ALJ credits
Claimant’s testimony to find and conclude that he last worked on July 22, 2025,
that he has not been released to work by his medical providers and that his
complete inability to work has resulted in an actual wage loss lasting more than
three work shifts. Based upon the evidence presented, the ALJ is persuaded
that Claimant has been “disabled” within the meaning of section 8-42-105, C.R.S.
8

beginning July 22, 2025. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999);
Hendricks v. Keebler Company, W.C. No. 4-373-392 (ICAO, June 11, 1999).
Thus, he is entitled to TTD benefits. Because the period of disability lasted
longer than two weeks from the day Claimant left work as a consequence of the
injury, he is entitled to recover disability benefits from the day he left work in this
case. See § 8-42-103(1)(b), C.R.S.
L. TTD benefits shall continue until the employee reaches maximum medical
improvement, returns to regular or modified-duty employment, is given a written
release by his attending physician to return to regular work or is given a written
release to modified duty and such modified duty is offered to Claimant, in writing,
and Claimant fails to begin such employment. See § 8-42-105 (3). Here, the
evidence presented supports the conclusion that none of the aforementioned
factors have been satisfied. Consequently, Respondent-Employer shall pay TTD
in accordance with C.R.S. § 8-42-105 (1) until such time that these benefits can
be terminated pursuant to statute. See § 8-42-105 (3) (a-d).
Claimant’s Average Weekly Wage and Concurrent Employment
M. The overall purpose of the average weekly wage (AWW) statute is to arrive
at a fair approximation of a claimant’s wage loss and diminished earning capacity
resulting from the industrial injury. See Campbell v. IBM Corp., 867 P.2d 77 (Colo.
App. 1993)2; National Fruit Prod. v. Crespin, 952 P.2d 1207 (Colo. App. 1997).
2 The claimant in Campbell suffered three periods of temporary disability and for each subsequent
period was earning a higher average weekly wage. The question resolved was whether Ms.
Campbell was entitled to temporary disability benefits based on the higher AWW she was earning
during each successive period of temporary disability. The Court held that it would be unjust to
calculate her disability benefits in 1986 and 1989 on her substantially lower earnings she was
making in 1979.
9

N. The best evidence of Claimant’s actual wage loss and therefore a fair
approximation of his diminished earning capacity at the time of his industrial
injury comes from his testimony at hearing. Claimant testified that at the time of
his work-related accident he was working 9 hours per day, 5 days a week for a
total of 45 hours. He noted that he was paid $28 per hour which equates to an
average weekly wage of $1,350. ($28/hr. x 45 hour/week = $1,350/week). The
ALJ credits Claimant’s testimony to find that this $1,350 figure most closely
approximates Claimant’s wage loss and diminished earning capacity at the time
of his July 22, 2025, work-related injury.
Penalties
O. Claimant seeks penalties against Respondent-Employer for failing to carry
Worker’s Compensation insurance pursuant to C.R.S. § 8-43-408. Section 8-43-
408(5), C.R.S. provides:
In addition to any compensation paid or ordered . . . an
employer who is not in compliance with the insurance provisions
of [the Act] at the time an employee suffers a compensable
injury, or occupational disease shall pay an amount equal to
twenty-five percent of the compensation or benefits to which the
employee is entitled to the Colorado uninsured employer fund
created in section 8-67-105.
P. Based upon the evidence presented, including Claimant’s testimony
surrounding Respondent-Employer’s actions of paying some lost wage benefits
after Claimant’s accident persuades the ALJ that Respondent-Employer was not
insured for workers’ compensation injuries on July 22, 2025. The penalty for
failure to insure only applies to indemnity benefits; it does not apply to medical
benefits. Industrial Commission v. Hammond, 77 Colo. 414, 236 P. 1006 (1925);
Jacobson v. Doan, 319 P.2d 975 (Colo. 1957); Wolford v. Support, Inc., W.C. No.
4-155- 231 (February 13, 1998). Although the ALJ is not aware of a case directly
10

on point, statutory interest is not properly considered “compensation or benefits”
within the meaning of § 8-43-408 (5). Interest is a statutory right intended to
secure claimants the present value of benefits to which they are entitled by
creating an equitable remedy for the lost time value of money during the accrual
period. Subsequent Injury Fund v. Trevethan, 809 P.2d 1098 (Colo. App. 1991).
Accordingly, interest is not included in the “penalty” amount Respondent-
Employer is ordered to pay pursuant to C.R.S. § 8-43-408 (5).
Q. Claimant is entitled to $900 in weekly or $128.57 in daily TTD benefits
beginning July 22, 2025, and continuing until such time that the TTD benefits can
be terminated in accordance with statute. See § 8-42-105 (3) (a-d). As of the
issuance of this order, Claimant is entitled to 288 days of TTD benefits for a total
TTD award of $37,028.16. ($128.57/day x 288 days = $37,028.16). Twenty- five
percent (25%) of the compensation awarded is $9,257.04, which sum shall be
sent to the Division of Workers’ Compensation Revenue Assessment Unit, 633
17th Street, Suite 400, Denver, CO 80202.
R. As Respondent-Employer was not insured for workers’ compensation liability
at the time of Claimant’s injury, § 8-43-408(2) of the Workers’ Compensation Act
requires Employer to pay to the trustee of the Division of Workers’ Compensation
(“Division”) an amount equal to the present value of all unpaid compensation or
benefits, computed at 4% per annum. In the alternative, Employer may file a
bond with the Division signed by two or more responsible sureties approved by
the Director or by some surety company authorized to do business in Colorado.
Employer may contact the Division Trustee for assistance with his obligations in
this regard. The Division Trustee may be contacted through the Division’s
customer service line at 303-318-8700 or by email to Mariya Cassin
mariya.cassin@state.co.us.
S. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
11

NOTE: This decision is final and not subject to appeal unless a full order is
requested. The request shall be made at the Office of Administrative Courts,
2864. S. Circle Drive, Suite 810, Colorado Springs, CO 80906 within ten (10)
working days of the date of service of this Summary Order. Section 8-43-215 (1),
C.R.S. Such a Request is a prerequisite to review under Section 8-43-301,
C.R.S.
If a party makes a request for a full order both parties shall submit a
proposed full order, containing specific findings of fact and conclusions of law
within five working days from the date of the request. The proposed full order
must be submitted by e-mail in Word or Rich Text format to OAC-
CSP@state.co.us. The proposed order shall also be submitted to opposing
counsel and unrepresented parties by e-mail, facsimile, or same day or next day
delivery.
So ordered this __6th___ day of May 2026.
/s/ Richard M. Lamphere____________
Richard M. Lamphere
Administrative Law Judge
